extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, combinatorialists, and graduate students interested in the culture and evaluation of mathematical research
extracted.subtask_description: Extract criteria for judging mathematical work and for choosing research directions, with emphasis on the contrast between problem-solving and theory-building (especially in combinatorics). Useful for assessing what makes results important, memorable, transmissible, or valuable across fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two cultures: problem-solvers vs theory-builders
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinction between mathematicians who regard their central aim as solving problems and those more concerned with building and understanding theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the two diagnostic statements Gowers gives: (i) 'The point of solving problems is to understand mathematics better.' (ii) 'The point of understanding mathematics is to become better able to solve problems.' The criterion is a practitioner's stated priority — whether their goal is understanding (theory-building) or solving problems (problem-solving). This categorization is an oversimplification but useful for explaining attitudes, priorities, and how one evaluates work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest via improvement of mathematical understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: One way to distinguish more interesting mathematical results is whether they 'improve our understanding of mathematics as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results that illuminate connections, reveal organizing principles, or explain phenomena beyond an isolated instance are judged more interesting. Solving a problem is more noteworthy if it contributes to broader understanding rather than being an isolated curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizability and economic explanation (communicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The results that will last are those 'that can be organized coherently and explained economically to future generations of mathematicians.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a theorem or paper, ask whether it fits into an organizing framework, whether it can be succinctly explained, and whether it aids transmission to future researchers. Lack of such organization makes long-term attention unlikely even for clever isolated results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of general principles and memorable ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Important ideas often appear not as precise theorems but as general principles of wide applicability which can be memorized and reused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess work for the presence of such principles (heuristics, probabilistic methods, concentration phenomena) that condense arguments and can be applied to many problems; these amplify a mathematician's power and aid transmission and reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance measured by introduction of new techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem or result is significant if it almost inevitably introduces a 'major new technique' or method that advances the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gowers cites the expectation that substantially improving bounds for Ramsey's function would require new global techniques. Evaluate whether solving a problem would create tools applicable beyond the single problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth as dependence on general principles rather than formal theorem chains
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth can be judged either by long formal chains of theorem dependence (theory-builders' view) or by the extent to which general principles introduced in proofs enable future results (problem-solvers' view).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing depth, consider whether results rely on many deep antecedents or whether they introduce widely useful heuristics/principles that unlock many subsequent problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of general goals and major open problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Having field-level goals or universally acknowledged important problems (e.g., P=NP, Riemann hypothesis analogues) contributes to a subject's direction and perceived importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a subfield has clearly articulated problems whose solutions would reflect major conceptual advances; such problems help justify work even if individual results look like puzzles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission criterion: does the result help future problem-solvers?
rubrics_metrics.description: For areas prioritizing problem-solving, a result's value relates to whether understanding it improves the problem-solving ability of future researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the ideas in a paper teach methods or principles that others can apply to new problems; results that are mostly isolated calculations with no transferable insight are less valuable for this metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-field impact: seven modes of interaction (i–vii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gowers lists seven ways area A can help area B, giving a graded rubric for cross-disciplinarity: (i) immediate useful consequence, (ii) consequence after work, (iii) A-proof resembles B-question so it can be adapted, (iv) solving A leads to tools in B of independent interest, (v) A provides useful analogous definitions for B, (vi) expertise in A provides habits of thought useful in B, (vii) A is close enough in spirit that good workers in A will likely do well in B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging cross-field significance, classify the link according to these modes; more direct links (i–iii) are immediately visible, while looser connections (iv–vii) may be substantial but less obvious. Use this to argue for the broader value of work that may not have immediate consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility and applications (practical justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: A branch can justify itself directly by practical applications (e.g., combinatorics' connection to computer science) or indirectly via connections to other mathematical areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether work has clear applications or useful connections (cryptography, communication theory, probability, number theory, Banach spaces, harmonic analysis) — these raise the field's perceived value beyond internal aesthetic reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for explicit organizing frameworks or classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Fields gain power when one can classify objects (e.g., colorings or graphs) or provide frameworks (e.g., Szemerédi's regularity lemma) that organize disparate examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether research contributes toward useful classifications or frameworks; Gowers stresses that finding more detailed/refined classifications is a general goal in graph theory and combinatorics, and such advances are highly valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudorandomness and 'random-like' modelling as a methodological criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Many combinatorial problems are best approached by viewing structures as composed of random-like pieces or by modeling with pseudorandom objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating combinatorial work, consider whether pseudorandom models and notions (e.g., uniform pairs, quasi-random graphs) are appropriately used or developed; success in modeling by randomness is a positive indicator of insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem selection: focus on problems embodying recurring difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing problems that encapsulate recurring difficulties or themes is valuable because solving them advances methods for a wide class of problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a proposed research problem by whether it isolates important recurring obstacles and thus serves as a vehicle for developing broadly useful techniques rather than being an isolated curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and career/practical consequences of cultural divides
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of communication between cultures (theory-building vs problem-solving) leads to undesirable practical consequences: unfair decisions affecting careers and misdirected pressure on students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating departments, hiring, or curriculum decisions, consider whether the balance of subfields and mutual understanding allow fair assessment of diverse mathematical styles; promoting communication is part of healthy field stewardship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research style: curiosity-driven exploratory work vs goal-directed problem pursuit
rubrics_metrics.description: Gowers records Atiyah's account of working by roaming 'in the mathematical waters'—following curiosity and emergent connections—versus starting with a fixed problem to solve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize both styles as valid: evaluate work in light of its approach. Curiosity-driven work may produce unexpected connections and is to be valued even when no particular target was set at the outset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristics/principles list for combinatorial thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Gowers lists concrete heuristic principles often used in combinatorics: (i) limited dependence among events can still allow joint occurrence, (ii) graphs are made of random-like pieces, (iii) count-solution problems can be attacked via Fourier coefficients of characteristic functions, (iv) many random-graph properties are equivalent and so define pseudo-randomness, (v) sequences of 0/1 eventually-zero can model separable Banach spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these heuristics as evaluation criteria for methods: presence, awareness, or development of such heuristics in a paper indicates that the author is situating work within the productive 'organizing principles' of the field. Examples (Erdős probabilistic method, Milman's concentration of measure, Szemerédi regularity) illustrate how such heuristics become powerful tools.
